Since we use the FP8 version, we test if this is caused by to low precision during the calculations. But we find the same behavior with the FP16 version. Llama 4 Maverick is the only model in our experiments that exhibits the problem of context rot. Context rot is a term introduces in Kelly Hong & Anton Troynikov (2025). They investigate an advanced Needle in the Haystack problem, including distractors and requiring the LLMs to find semantic similarity instead of exact term matching. They find that the accuracy often starts to decrease with 10 k input tokens and more. Meta claims that Llama 4 Maverick has a context length 1 M (Llama 4 Scout even 10 M), where other models often are limited to 128 k, 32 k or less. We limited our input token length to 32 k in most cases and reached this limit multiple times. We find it remarkable, that Llama 4 Maverick already shows context rot at inputs of length 10 k — 100 times shorter than their context window. Levy et al. (2024) demonstrate that LLMs’ reasoning performance can degrade at much shorter input lengths than their technical maximum. They also show that Mistral achieves the highest accuracy when the relevant information is positioned at the end of the prompt. However, it remains unclear how these findings apply to our experiments, as we do not include irrelevant information. 6.2.4.1 Page identification 6.2.4.1.1 Binary classification Figure 6.2 shows the amount of correct (matching) and incorrect classifications by Llama 4 Maverick for the binary classification tasks ordered by target type and method. For page identification, LLMs sometimes misclassify tables with similar content as the target classes, while the term frequency method can be misled by common terms and high float density. We suggest the need for improved weighting schemes like BM25 or boolean indicators. In information extraction, using in-company examples improves extraction perfromance. Excessive homogeneity can reduce performance, if examples come from another companies documents. OpenAI models demonstrate, that LLMs perform well even without strict schemas if their parameter count is high enough. Overall, the analysis highlights the importance of careful example selection, robust schema design, and thorough ground truth validation to minimize errors. 6.3 Practical Implications and Limitations This section discusses the results from an engineers perspective, focusing on implications for the planned HITL application and possible improvements. 6.3.1 Page identification A detailed view on the results shows, that a combination of two LLMs would be necessary, to get the best results for each target class. A more general approach would be using Llama 4 Scout for multi-class classification for all target classes. If there is little VRAM Ministral-8B also does a decent job in multi-class classification. We recommend, to refine the page range, using a term frequency based approach, for efficiency reasons discussed in Section 6.3.1.4. It is an important prerequisite, that any method used for page refinement has a recall of 1.0. Otherwise, a user potentially has to inspect the whole document and no improvement is reached compared to the manual processing. Afterwards the LLM can be used to perform a multi-class classification on the top k pages from the ranking, that results from the term frequency approach. The page, that gets the highest confidence score from the LLM should be used for the information extraction task. The confidence score ranking should be kept for presenting alternative pages, if the chosen one is incorrect. Figure 6.6 illustrates our recommendation to begin information extraction immediately, without requiring a mandatory human confirmation of the selected page. If the user reviews the results and notices an incorrect page, alternative pages can be manually checked in order of their confidence score ranking. Pages that have already been classified should be saved in a vector database along with their class labels, enabling their reuse in future classification tasks and enhancing overall system performance. For in-context learning, examples should be selected based on vector similarity and should utilize in-company examples. We recommend populating the vector database document by document initially, before moving to batch processing. Figure 6.6: Showing the information extraction process in a HITL application. We propose to include user action only after the information extraction. If a wrong page is selected, this can be fixed and extraction runs again. Wrong extracted values and handling unknown row identifiers should be done in one place. 6.3.1.1 Transfering the system to new problems Expanding the system to new application areas should be straightforward, even for non-expert users. For the term frequency approach, a pipeline can be established where users input a list of keywords and receive a page ranking based on term frequency metrics. Users can refine the keyword list or directly select relevant pages to create a ground truth. If additional metrics are needed (such as float frequency), the system can automatically train a random forest classifier. Alternatively, users can provide documents along with a list indicating which pages contain the desired information. This data can serve as the foundation for a retrieval-augmented few-shot classifier, which will improve as more pages are classified. 6.3.1.2 Limitations of transfer The term frequency and LLM classification might perform worse, if the information of interest, is just making up a small part of the pages’ content. If the information is placed in a table, we can use a visual table detection model, to identify all tables. We show in the Appendix 12.3.2.2, that this is a promising approach. Then we can use the retrieval augmented few-shot approach to identify, which table is the correct one. If the information is not placed in a table, but part of a regular sentence, it might get difficult to find the correct page with this approach. Maybe the TOC approach could be used for page range refinement in this case, if the information is found in a section with known heading. 6.3.1.3 Possible improvement 6.3.1.3.1 Term frequency approach Drawing on the error analysis for the term frequency approach (see Section 6.2.1.2), we recommend using either the sum of boolean indicators or the sum of BM25 scores instead of the normalized sum of term frequencies. Alternatively, each individual indicator could be used as a feature for the random forest classifier; however, this would require a larger training and test dataset to avoid overfitting due to the increased number of features. 6.3.1.3.2 Table of contents understanding approach H. Li, Gao, et al. (2023) applied a few-shot learning strategy for the TOC approach, whereas we implemented only a zero-shot strategy. With greater expertise and more concrete examples included in the prompt, this method would likely achieve better results, as reported in Section 5.1.2. Additionally, they used OpenAI’s GPT-4 for the TOC understanding task, which has significantly more parameters than Ministral-8B. It would be worthwhile to investigate whether Qwen3-235B performs better with text-based TOC. 6.3.1.4 Energy usage and runtime The fastest and least energy consuming strategy, using only LLMs, is to use a small model as Ministral-8B-Instruct for the multi-class approach. This is more effective than running three binary classifications. An alternative approach could be to binary predict if the page is of any target type and then perform a classification, which type exactly the page is of. But this would probably consume as much energy as the multi-class approach, because we have to provide a balanced amount of examples for each class. The results of the multi-class strategy are good enough to run it right away. In both strategies the k required for perfect recall is three, using the Ministral-8B-Instruct model10. Nevertheless, it is more promising, to reduce the number of pages, to classify with the LLM in the first place. This can be achieved, by running the term-frequency approach first to refine the page range, and then use the LLM approach. 6.3.1.4.1 Compare with manual page identification The manual approach is the slowest. We identified the pages of interest for all target classes in ten random documents for the benchmark. We used the TOC and the search function to find key words like Aktiva or Bilanz. Anyhow, it is almost as fast as the full multi-classification using Llama 4 Scout, while consuming eight times less energy. Comparing it to Ministral-8B-Instruct it takes three times longer but consumes less then half of the energy. Thus, comparing full manual processing and full LLM-driven classifiaction, a benefit of the LLM approach would be, that the human user could perform another task, while the LLM is classifying a whole batch of documents and that it frees the user from a boring task. But in terms of energy consumption the manual approach is still more efficient. Not taken into account for this comparison so far are factors as: Costs to buy and maintain hardware (i.e. a GPU cluster). Higher costs per runtime/token if the LLM compute is purchased from cloud providers. The payment and insurance costs for a human (e.g. student coworker). The training time and energy consumption for training either a LLM (probably done by the LLM provider). a human (growing up, getting educated). The energy consumed to produce the hardware. The argument that probably will be most important to many CEOs are costs. The costs presented in table 5.3 only include the costs for energy. To calculate the cloud computing costs it is important to know, how many tokens are processed. The number of response tokens per page identified can be limited to one and thus is neglectable. In contrast, the counts of input tokens needed to classify a single page fall into the range od \(10^3\) to \(10^4\) tokens. The exact number depends on the number of examples provided for in-context learning. Here are two examples: binary classifiaction wit 3 random examples: 6.5 k input tokens multi-class classification with 3 random examples: 11 k input tokens If we assume, one uses GPT-4.1-mini hosted in the Azure cloud instead of running the LLM locally, we estimate a price of 118.80 € for the multi-class classification of 1_000 documents, assuming a cost of 0.4 $ per 1 M input tokens and 27 pages per document. For a human employee we have to add their payment and insurance costs to the energy costs. Even for a student worker this will sum up to 0.5 CENTS per second. This totals in 319.80 € for identifying the target pages for 1_000 documents. This assumes 15 € per hour payment and 10 % additional costs for insurance. 6.3.1.5 Conclusion In summary, combining term frequency-based page refinement with LLM-driven multi-class classification offers an efficient and accurate approach for page identification in financial documents. Storing classified pages in a vector database and leveraging in-context learning further enhances system performance and adaptability. While limitations exist when relevant information is sparse or embedded in non-tabular text, integrating visual table detection and retrieval-augmented strategies can address these challenges. Regarding energy usage and runtime, our analysis demonstrates that smaller LLMs such as Ministral-8B-Instruct provide a highly efficient solution for multi-class page identification, outperforming manual methods in speed and energy consumption. While manual identification remains less resource-intensive, it is significantly slower and less scalable. Factoring in hardware, cloud computing, and personnel costs, automated LLM-based approaches offer substantial economic advantages, especially for large-scale document processing. Prioritizing page range refinement before LLM classification further optimizes resource use, making the system both cost-effective and environmentally responsible. 6.3.2 Information extraction It remains unclear whether the 2% of incorrectly extracted numeric values are due to unhandled currency units or other factors. One possible explanation is that faulty text extraction may cause numeric values to be concatenated. If this is the case, it raises the question of whether further investment in advanced table extraction methods is warranted. To further assess extraction performance, we evaluate text extracts from various Python libraries, including advanced solutions such as Azure Document Intelligence and Docling, both capable of table detection and extraction. We also experimented with providing Markdown instead of plain text — generated by Docling and pymupdf — to preserve table structure information, and tested an OCR-based approach using tesseract. Table 6.3 presents the aggregated results for the best prompting method with Qwen3-235B across all input types. No improvement was observed over the results obtained with text extracted by pdfium. In fact, performance declined when using Markdown generated by pymupdf or text produced via OCR. Notably, Qwen3-235B performed equally well with Markdown generated by Docling as with other plain text extracts, indicating that the issue is not specific to the Markdown format. Therfore, we advocate prioritizing the development of end-to-end data pipelines to eliminate the need for document parsing altogether. This enables straightforward evaluation of the results and processing in down stream tasks. But it excludes reports of well known companies as BVG and BSR. For the final system we intend to add an additional classifier between the page identification and information extraction steps, that detects what granularity the asset table is reported in. Then a proper schema is applied in the information extraction task. This will still not use all information found in all tables. Therefore, we intend to access, which row identifiers do not match and extract the corresponding rows in a separate json formatted list. We have to test, if this can be performed in a single step or with another information extraction prompt. Another approach would be to use guided instead of restricted decoding. For this strategy one can pass the description of the target structure within the prompt and just enforce the generation of valid json code. We unwillingly made first tests with this approach, because we were not able to use a strict schema with the models of OpenAI. We describe our findings about this in Section 6.2.2.5. 6.3.2.0.2 Conclusion To summarize, we recommend to invest resources into an end-to-end supply of machine-readable information and good user experience instead of system that achieves perfect extraction results. We believe that the performance as it is is already sufficient. Especially if the document extraction database is build document by document to use a RAG architecture to take advantage of in-context learning with in-company examples. 6.3.3 Error rate guidance Implementing a measure to guide users’ attention, indicating which predictions require review and which can be trusted, would be highly beneficial for the information extraction task. Verifying the extracted values for a single table can take up to three minutes, amounting to 300 minutes for the entire sample. This process is up to four times faster than manually transferring all values. Choosing a smaller model that completes in 2:30 minutes rather than 3:00 minutes does not significantly accelerate the workflow, as error checking must still be performed on all values. Error checking could be omitted if perfect results are achieved, or if a reliable criterion is identified that allows predictions to be grouped into bins with a near-zero error rate. One promising criterion for this purpose is the company that published the document. As demonstrated in 6.2.2.2, information extraction already yields error-free results for many companies’ documents. If the table structure remains consistent, similar empirical error rates can be expected for future documents. However, some companies in our sample have introduced structural changes, such as reporting values in T€, which affect error rates. Additionally, we recommend selecting a threshold value close to zero, rather than exactly zero, to define groups of predictions with sufficiently low empirical error rates. Otherwise, these groups may become too unstable. More sophisticated confidence measures could also be explored, but we are not optimistic that they will provide substantially better discrimination. 6.3.3.0.1 Conclusion Overall, the system effectively distinguishes between correctly and incorrectly classified pages, enabling the creation of a ranking that helps users quickly identify the most promising alternatives when misclassifications occur. Although this functionality may be seldom required due to the high precision achieved, it provides a valuable safety net for edge cases. For information extraction, further segmentation could enhance the utility of confidence scores, but alternative grouping criteria may ultimately prove more effective and could reduce reliance on confidence scores altogether. 6.4 Not covered This section briefly outlines topics that were not addressed within the scope of this thesis. 6.4.0.0.1 Table extraction and document parsing Classical libraries and modern machine learning models are available for table extraction from documents. We evaluated tabula as a traditional solution, but its performance was unsatisfactory — particularly for tables without borders, where it often failed to correctly identify rows and columns. We were unable to implement more recent models for this task, such as visual LLMs. Although promising results have been reported for these approaches, user-friendly implementations for transformers or vLLM are still often lacking. Notably, our method performed well using basic text extraction, so we did not pursue more advanced extraction tools or models further. 6.4.0.0.2 Multi-page tables Methods for handling multi-page tables were not investigated, as multi-page tables were only encountered for GuV tables. Addressing this will be a software engineering challenge for the final system. Document layout analysis models could be used to identify related pages, allowing text extracts to be concatenated for subsequent information extraction. 6.4.0.0.3 Optical character recognition For documents consisting solely of scanned images, OCR is an essential preprocessing step, as all approaches in this thesis rely on text extraction. OCR systems typically include document layout analysis to manage multi-column layouts and tables. 6.4.0.0.4 Fine-tuning LLMs can be fine-tuned for specific tasks, such as generating text in a particular style or performing classification. For classification, a softmax pooling layer is added. The object detection model Yolo 12 used in this work is an example of a fine-tuned model for table detection. We did not perform fine-tuning with LLMs, opting instead for in-context learning to assess its sufficiency. It would be valuable to estimate how many in-context prompts are required before the energy consumption for additional token processing exceeds that of fine-tuning. 6.4.0.0.5 Training an encoder-only model Training a smaller encoder-only model, such as BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers), may be more efficient for classification tasks. However, unlike LLMs, such models would need to be retrained for each new classification task, necessitating the creation of a dedicated training dataset. 6.4.0.0.6 UX design study A UX design study has not yet been conducted. Such a study could be valuable in the near future to develop an application based on the information extraction processes explored in this thesis, tailored for employees of RHvB. Early involvement of potential users is beneficial for successful software development (User Participation in Software Development Projects – Communications of the ACM, 2010), helping to avoid unnecessary features and cumbersome workflows, while also increasing motivation and willingness to adopt the final AI-driven product (Errida & Lotfi, 2021). 6.4.0.0.7 Advanced prompting techniques Advanced prompting strategies, such as Chain-of-Thought, ReAct, or Self-Consistency (Prompt Engineering Guide, n.d.), encourage step-by-step reasoning and deeper effort. However, given the strong performance already achieved and initial signs of context rot, we do not recommend further investment in advanced prompt template development at this stage. 6.5 Ethical & Practical Considerations 6.5.1 Ethical Considerations Extracting numeric information is distinct from decision-making and is unlikely to introduce human-discriminating bias. Automation of information extraction may replace roles requiring lower qualifications; however, at RHvB, such positions no longer exist. Thus, this automation primarily serves to enhance efficiency, allowing staff to focus on more complex tasks. According to current regulations, individuals should not be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing (such as algorithms) that are legally binding or significantly affect them. But the AI Act is likely not applicable here, as no decisions are made at the individual level. Furthermore, errors, that decisions could be based on, should be catched by an employee in the HITL approach before they have down stream implications. 6.5.2 Computational Constraints Information extraction using LLMs is computationally intensive and ideally requires GPU acceleration. For example, running Qwen3-235B-A32B-Instruct-FP8, the model yielding the best extraction results, requires four H200 GPUs. Similarly, Llama 4 Scout, which performed best in page identification, also needs four H200 GPUs. Loading these models ad hoc is impractical due to setup times of approximately 30 minutes each. In contrast, Ministral-8B and Qwen3-8B can operate on a single NVIDIA 5090 RTX or A100. 6.5.3 Generalizability Scope The approach evaluated here is likely applicable to annual reports from other companies. However, if the information of interest occupies only a small portion of a page, the framework may require adaptation. Page identification may also become more challenging when only a single keyword is available for search. 6.5.4 PDF Extraction Limitations Pdfminer indicates that the text from certain annual reports, such as those from IBB and Berlinovo, should not be extracted, as noted in the PDF metadata. Nevertheless, we utilized these text extracts for our study. 6.6 Outlook To implement the proposed system at RHvB, several infrastructural challenges must be addressed. With the transition away from local infrastructure, migration to a secure cloud environment is required, including establishing protected connections to the Berlin intranet and ensuring confidential data is processed securely. In the short term, the strategy does not yet incorporate GPU resources. Key areas for improvement include enhancing system flexibility and expanding the range of supported use cases. This involves developing solutions for users to manage unknown row identifiers and automating the process of populating the RAG component with examples for identification and extraction tasks. A user interface must be developed to guide users through the workflow, enabling error correction and the handling of unknown row identifiers. Additionally, procedures for managing new entries need to be defined: whether to aggregate them with existing row identifiers, extend the database of known entities, or introduce a new hierarchy level to accommodate more granular reporting by housing cooperatives. We also plan to establish a machine learning operations pipeline to monitor system health and facilitate ongoing benchmarking. This will allow for systematic evaluation of new models and, crucially, assessment of whether new examples provided by employees may negatively impact system performance. Furthermore, we intend to request annual reports in XBRL (eXtensible Bbusiness Reporting Language) format. Since 2012, German companies have been required to submit reports in this machine-readable format for tax purposes (§ 5b EStG), although RHvB has not yet utilized this resource. Our goal is to develop a robust, error-free solution for this specific task based on XBRL data. 6.7 Summary This chapter critically evaluated the performance, limitations, and practical implications of {LLM}s and term frequency-based approaches for page identification and information extraction in financial documents. The error analysis highlighted strengths and weaknesses of both methods, emphasizing the importance of robust schema design, careful example selection, and thorough ground truth validation. Practical recommendations are provided for system implementation, including the integration of HITL workflows, energy and cost considerations, and strategies for expanding the system to new use cases. Ethical and computational constraints are discussed, with attention resource requirements and the impact of automation on the workforce. The chapter concludes that combining term frequency-based refinement with LLM-driven classification offers an efficient, scalable, and adaptable solution, while also outlining areas for future improvement and topics not covered in the current work. 7 Conclusion

7 Conclusion This thesis investigated the use of LLMs and related approaches for extracting financial information from German annual reports, with a focus on supporting the audit processes at the RHvB. We addressed three main research questions: how to effectively locate specific information in financial reports using LLMs, how to extract this information accurately, and whether additional information from the extraction process can guide users in verifying results. Our results demonstrate that LLMs can be used effectively to identify relevant pages and extract structured financial data, achieving performance close to or exceeding human benchmarks in many cases. Combining LLMs with term-frequency-based methods further improves efficiency, reducing computational costs without sacrificing performance. The experiments also show that open-weight models are viable alternatives to proprietary solutions, especially when data privacy is a concern. We found that LLMs are capable of extracting multiple numeric values from complex tables, matching entities, and handling missing or ambiguous data accurately. The use of confidence scores for guiding users in HITL workflows, highlighting which values require verification and which can be trusted, is found to be less successful. Other extraction metadata might help to achieve this goal. Our findings have practical implications for automating information retrieval in regulatory and financial contexts, particularly where documents are unstructured and machine readability is limited. The developed framework and evaluation strategies can be adapted to similar tasks in other domains. Future work could explore further improvements in system architectures, prompt engineering, and integration with advanced document layout analysis. Expanding the scope to more heterogeneous document types and new tasks, as well as refining HITL strategies, will help ensure robust and scalable solutions for real-world applications.

8 Appendix A - Page identification report The first research question asks, how LLMs can be used, to effectively locate specific information in a financial report. The task for this thesis is to identify the pages where the balance sheet (Bilanz) and the profit-and-loss-and-statement (Gewinn- und Verlustrechnung, GuV) are located. The balance sheet is composed of two tables showing the assets (Aktiva) and liabilities (Passiva) of a company. Often, these two tables are on separate pages. Hereafter, the German terms Aktiva, Passiva and GuV will be used. 8.1 Baseline: Regex Code data_page_identification_regex <- readRDS("data_storage/page_identification_regex.rds") metrics <- data_page_identification_regex$metrics metric_summaries <- data_page_identification_regex$metric_summaries metrics_by_company_and_type <- data_page_identification_regex$metrics_by_company_and_type metrics_plot_regex_page_identification <- metrics %>% bind_rows() %>% pivot_longer( cols = -c(package, method, classification_type), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value" ) %>% filter(metric %in% c( # "acc", "precision", "recall", "F1")) %>% ggplot() + geom_jitter(aes(x = method, y = value, color = package), alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2, height = 0) + facet_grid(metric~classification_type) + scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 30)) + theme( legend.position = "bottom" ) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) # creating combi table df_list <- list() for (type in c("Aktiva", "Passiva", "GuV")) { df_temp <- metric_summaries[type][[1]] %>% mutate_if( is.numeric, ~ifelse( . == max(., na.rm = TRUE), paste0("**", format(round(., 3), nsmall=3), "**"), format(round(., 3), nsmall=3) ) ) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = c(precision, recall, F1)) %>% mutate( precision = paste(precision_mean, "±", precision_sd), recall = paste(recall_mean, "±", recall_sd), F1 = paste(F1_mean, "±", F1_sd), ) %>% select(-ends_with("_mean")) %>% select(-ends_with("_sd")) %>% mutate_all(~str_remove(., " ± NA")) %>% arrange(desc(method)) %>% mutate(.before = 2, type = type) # rownames(df_temp) <- df_temp$method df_list[[type]] <- df_temp } df_combined <- bind_rows(df_list) %>% bold_value_in_table() The first approach presented in this section is, to use a key word list and regex (regular expression) to filter out irrelevant pages. It is setting the performance baseline for the following approaches. Building a sound regular expression often is an iterative process. In a first approach a very simple regex was implemented. To increase the recall to 1.0 the regular expression was extended11. This second regex is called exhaustive regex. In a third attempt minor changes have been made to the exhaustive regex to increase the precision without decreasing the recall. This regular expression is called exhausitve regex restricted. The regular expressions can be found in the appendix (see section 12.5). Table 8.1 shows the mean performance for precision, recall and F1 for the three regular expressions for the three types of pages to identify12. It was possible to create a regular expression that has a high recall for all target types. The precision is low for all tested regular expressions and target types. Figure 8.1 gives insight into performance differences between the companies. There is only one document from Berlin Energie und Netzholding where the GuV is not identified except with the exhausitve regex restricted13. The regular expressions have been tested on the texts extracted with multiple Python libraries. The reported standard deviations are very small. This means that there are no substantial differences in the extracted texts on a word level14. But table 12.1 in section 12.3.1 shows that there are differences in the extraction speed. Li, Gao, et al. (2023) use this approach with long documents as a first step to determine a page range of interest. If the predicted page range is correct and narrow, this approach is more efficient than processing the whole document with a LLM directly. The TOC in a PDF document can be embedded in a standardized, machine readable format or be presented in varying, human readable forms of text on any page. Of course there are documents without any TOC. Thus, the task is investigated based on two different input data formats In one case the LLM is provided with text extracted from the beginning of the document. In the other case the LLM is provided with the Markdown formatted version of the machine readable TOC embedded in the document. Subsection 8.2.1 shows the results for the text based approach. Subsection 8.2.1.0.2 shows the results for the approach, using the embedded TOC. Additionally, each approach is performed three times with minor changes in the prompt. The prompts used for both approaches can be found at 12.4.1. The prompt was adjusted two times to tackle shortcomings in the results. The first change adds the information, that assets and liabilities are part of the balance sheet. It is the balance sheet, that is listed in the TOC - not the assets or liabilities itself. The second change specifies the information, that assets and liabilities are often on separated pages, into, liabilities often are found on the page after the assets. The code can be found in: “benchmark_jobs/page_identification/toc_extraction_mistral.ipynb” “benchmark_jobs/page_identification/toc_extraction_qwen.ipynb” 8.2.1 Details for the approaches 8.2.1.0.1 Text based H. Li, Gao, et al. (2023) used the TOC to identify the pages of interest. In their approach the table of contents is extracted from the text. Based on their observation, that the TOC in ACFRs is found within the initial 165 lines of the converted document (H. Li, Gao, et al., 2023, p. 20), they use the first 200 lines of text. My initial expectation was to find the TOC within the first five pages. Often there are way less than 200 lines of text on the five first pages (see Figure 8.2). In my approach the first step is to prompt the LLM to identify and extract the TOC in a given text extract^[The prompt can be found in section 12.4.1]. For the same documents Ministral 2410 8B finds^[The strings extracted in this step have not been checked in detail.] 63 strings that should represent a table of contents among the first five pages. 68 strings that should represent a table of contents among the first 200 lines. Two classification approaches are presented. On the one hand, a binary classification is used three times, to predict, if the text extract is including an Aktiva, Passiva or GuV table, once at a time. In this case the LLM is forced to answer with either yes or no. On the other hand, the LLM performed a \acr{mcc]. For the MCC (multi-class classification) the LLM is forced to answer Aktiva, Passiva, GuV or other. The prompts can be found in appendix in section 12.4.2. The different classification tasks are combined with different prompting strategies. A zero shot approach is setting the baseline. In a second approach the excerpt of the relevant law is provided with the context. Additionally, three few shot approaches are used. In the few shot approaches text examples and a correct classification for the text examples are provided. Figure 8.8 shows how many examples the LLM gets provided, depending on the classification type and chosen parameter n_example17. For both approaches three example selection strategies are implemented. First, random examples for each page type get sampled from the truth dataset. Second, a vector database provides the entries that are closest to the target text for each page type. Third, the vector database just provides the texts that are closest to the target text without considering the page type of the examples returned. For the binary classification task the LLM is provided with more examples for the target type than for other types. Thus, the number of examples and tokens is reduced. This should reduce the runtime as well. On the same time the LLM should get enough information about the structure and contents of the target class and some information how it differs from other big tables or general text pages. For the MCC the same amount of every possible class is provided. Thus, the relation between the parameter n_examples and the number of tokens to process is stronger for the n_random_examples and n_rag_examples strategies. The approach is inspired by TF-IDF - a technique commonly used for information retrieval. It is similar to the baseline approach, because it uses a key word list and regular expressions to count terms and floats. But it is more flexible because the works in the key word list are not mandatory. This makes the approach robust against issues in the text extracts for single key words. The key word list is generated removing the stop words from the law about Aktiva, Passiva and GuV. The key words from the regex approach are added, e.g. GuV and Gewinn- und Verlustrechnung. Since real life representations of those target types never contain all entries, it is not possible to include most of those words in a strict regex search as presented in the first approach. This approach sums the counts of each word from the key word list per page in a first variable. In a second variable it counts the number of floats on each page. These two variables are then divided by the number of words found on the page. These densities are used to rank all pages from a single document. This is done with a unique key word list for each target type. A random forest is trained to determine which density should be weighted to what amount. Because of the imbalanced data set undersampling is used when the training data set is created23. A single random forest is trained because the density of floats and specific words is assumed to be similar. The actual type of the page is not taken into account. The model just knows if the page is a page of any target type, based on the term and float density. This trippels the data points of the target class. This single random forest performs much better than random forests that are trained using the dataset for each target type separatly. The performance is tested on all data points not included in the undersampled train dataset. Thus the test dataset is again highly imbalanced. The random forest performs a binary classification task. But instead of the actual classifications, the predicted scores are used to rank the pages. Instead of precision or recall the metric used for the evaluation is top k recall. It is of interest which value of k is required to get a recall of 100 %. 9 Appendix B - Information extraction report The second research question asks, how LLMs can be used, to effectively extract specific information from a financial report. The task for this thesis is to extract the numeric values for the assets (Aktiva) table, which is part of the balance sheet (Bilanz). Hereafter, the German term Aktiva will be used. We are limiting the scope even further than in Subsection 5.1, because it takes more time to manually create the first reference dataset. 9.1 Baseline: Regex The baseline for the table extraction task is set by an approach using regular expressions on the text extract. Figure 9.1 shows the performance of this approach. In the first row (A) the percentage of correct predicted numeric values and the percentage of total correct responses is shown. The second row (B) shows the precision, recall and F1 score for identifying a value as missing and thus predicting null. The percentage of total correct responses is calculated as \[ percentage\_correct\_total = \frac{n_{correct\_numeric} + n_{missing\_true\_positive}}{n_{total\_entries}} \] with \(n_{total\_entries} = 58\) . This implies that the correct prediction of missing values has more influence for tables, that have only a few numeric values in the ground truth. The minimal number of numeric values in a tables is ten. Figure 14.1 shows, that the percentage of total correct responses is not a sufficient metric, because responses that only predicted null can have a high score if there are only a few numeric values in the ground truth table. 9.1.0.0.1 Performance In each frame there are two groups of two box-plots. The left group is showing the performance on real Aktiva tables. The right group shows the performance on synthetic Aktiva tables. Within the group the green (left) box shows the performance on text extracted with the pdfium library. The peach colored (right) box shows the performance on text extracted with the pymupdf library. Figure 9.1 shows, that the regex approach performs better24 on the synthetic tables compared to the real tables. Even though, the performance is not perfect and more consistent on the text extracted with pymupdf compared to pdfium. In contrast, the used text extraction library has no noticeable influence on the real Aktiva tables. Aktiva tables that should allow to investigate the influence certain characteristics of tables on the extraction task. We systematically created Aktiva tables that vary over the following characteristics: n_columns: Number of columns the numeric values are distributed over ranging from 2 to 4. header_span: Span in the header rows. thin: Including just a subset of all possible entries for a Aktiva table. unit_in_first_cell: Is the currency unit (e.g. T€) given in the beginning of the table instead for each column. enumeration: Are the rows numerated following the schema in the legal text. many_line_breaks: Limiting the character length for the row descriptions to 50 to introduce line breaks. shuffle_rows: The order of the rows within lower hierarchies can vary. text_around: There is some random text before and after the table on the generated page. sum_same_line: Summed values are in the same line as single values if there are more than two columns. unit: Eight different currency units from. E.g.: €, TEUR, Mio. € input_format: Table is exported as PDF, HTML or Markdown document. This results in 49152 tables. A sample of 10 % is used for the extraction task. The header_span and text_around are only varied for the PDF format. 9.2.2.0.2 Extraction task overview For the table extraction task with synthetic Aktiva tables 17 open source models from 6 model families have been benchmarked. There have been the same seven methods tested with each LLM as described in section 9.2. Each method was used twice, because in one trial the LLM is prompted to respect the currency units and in the other trail it is not. This results in 531 files, that hold the results of 4_915 table extractions each. For the investigation of potential predictors influences the random forest is generated with a sample of 50_000 of these 68_810 results and finally, the SHAP values are calculated with 2_000 rows of data. 9.2.2.0.3 Performance Table 9.9 shows the best performing combination of LLM and prompting strategy for each model family. The results are sorted by their mean percentage of total correct predictions. We only compare results for table extractions that work with a PDF document based table here. For every model family there is at least one model-method combination that performed better than the regex baseline. For the synthetic table extraction task the baseline is 0.966. 68 from 129 model-method combinations perform better than this baseline. There has been no model that performed better than this baseline with the zero_shot or static_example method. Table 9.9 shows, that Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct performs best. Llama 4 Scout also performs very good but is three times faster. Table 9.10 shows three small LLMs that also beat the median threshold for the synthetic table extraction task. But we would not prefer the Qwen3-8B model over the Llama Scout model, because its speed advantage is to small, compared to the performance decrease. But if there is limited VRAM available the Qwen3 model is a good choice. It can run well with 40 GB VRAM. The Llama Scout needs 640 GB VRAM to run well29. Detail: Figure 14.24 shows, that Llama 3.3 70B never manages to reduce the spread in the numeric prediction performance. 10 Appendix C - Error rate guidance report The side research question asks, if it is possible to guide the users attention to predictions that have a higher empirical rate of errors. In this thesis we focus on the confidence score calculated from the reported log probabilities. The formula for the confidence score is given in Equation (3.1). 10.1 Page identification 10.1.1 Binary classification Code target_type <- "Aktiva" df_filtered <- df_binary %>% filter( classification_type == target_type, n_examples<=3 ) %>% arrange(desc(f1_score)) df_temp <- df_filtered[1,"predictions"][[1]][[1]] %>% as_tibble() df_flipped_score <- df_temp %>% mutate( confidence_score = if_else(predicted_type == "no", 1-confidence_score, confidence_score), is_aktiva = str_detect(type, target_type) ) model_name_best_f1_aktiva <- df_filtered[1, "model"] method__best_f1_aktiva <- df_filtered[1, "method"] We investigate the relation between the reported confidence for an answer and its correctness, to check if it is possible to inform humans in the loop about results they should double check and which results they can trust. The LLM just returns one prediction and its confidence30 for the binary classification task. We calculate its confidence as \(confidence = exp(logprob)\), if the answer is yes. And we calculate its confidence as \(confidence = 1-exp(logprob)\), if the the answer is no, Figure 10.1 shows the distribution of reported confidence score for the binary classification with target type Aktiva for all table types grouped by their correctness for Ministral-8B-Instruct-2410. One can see that the predictions are very accurate making just 13 mistakes for 4981 predictions. The reported confidence for answer yes is showing a wide spread from around 0.25 to 1.0. This is true for the answer no as well. Most wrong decisions are made for responses that have a reported confidence in the range from 0.25 to 0.75. But there are more correct answers in this range as well. It never misclassifies GuV or Passiva31 as Aktiva. But it with shows some not recalled Aktiva tables and is predicting some of the pages of majority class, with not further described content and structure, as Aktiva. Synthetic tables 11.3.0.0.1 Hypotheses Table 11.4 shows some unsupported hypotheses for predictors with strong effects. The observations suggest, that prompting the model to respect the currency units is decreasing its performance to predict the correct numeric values. This is understandable, if the task is reflected properly and we made a mistake there, when we formulated our hypothesis. If the model is not prompted to respect the currency units, it is presented with examples that just copy over the numeric values. And it gets evaluated if it copied the values correctly. If the model is prompted to respect the currency units, it is presented with examples, where the values not only get copied but also transformed. And they get evaluated if they do the transformation correct as well. Thus the task is harder, if numeric values should be respected and the effect is having a negative direction. Figure 11.2 shows that the transformation task is handled best, if the examples are provided with the top_n_rag strategy. It does not work with the zero_shot strategy. It also shows, that the performance is lower with the PDF input_format and that the models have difficulties, if the unit_multiplier is one million. This also shows a strong effect and is strongest for the PDF input_format. This is a general effect.
